_comment: Model registry — the single source of truth for which inference models the
scanner can run under. Read by shared/models.ts (TypeScript stages) and by
run.sh / diff.sh / seed-upstream.sh (bash, via node), so the three can never
Adding a model is a data change, not a code change: append one entry to
`targets`. Nothing under tools/scanner/*/src/ needs to know it exists.
A target's KEY is also its run-artifact namespace: runs/<key>/<stage>/.
Key on the model, not the vendor — api.openai.com serves luna, terra and sol,
and each needs its own isolated run tree to be comparable.

luna.label: GPT-5.6 Luna
luna.notes: GPT-5.x reasoning models reject max_tokens with a 400 and are inconsistent about accepting non-default sampling values, so sampling is omitted and steering happens through the prompt. base_url null means the SDK default, https://api.openai.com/v1. Requires api.openai.com on the environment's egress allowlist.

terra.label: GPT-5.6 Terra
terra.notes: Middle tier of the GPT-5.6 family, same endpoint and key as luna. $2.50/$15 per MTok against luna's $1.00/$6.00. Added 2026-07-29 because every run to date has used the family's cheapest tier: docs/'Cybersecurity models pricing research' records luna as 'the smallest step up available' from qwen on cost grounds, so model capability has never been isolated as a variable.

sol.label: GPT-5.6 Sol
sol.notes: Top tier of the GPT-5.6 family, same endpoint and key as luna. $5.00/$30 per MTok, ~5x luna on input. Rated 96.7% on OpenAI's internal CTF suite, which they describe as saturated — read it as 'not capability-limited on security reasoning', not as a percentage of anything. See the pricing research doc's caveats before treating that number as a ranking.

luna-fixed.label: GPT-5.6 Luna (post-fix arm)
luna-fixed.notes: Same model as luna. A separate key so the run-5 artifacts in runs/luna/ stay untouched while the same model is re-measured with the 2026-07-29 fixes in force. Exists to separate 'the fixes helped' from 'the model tier helped' — without it, a terra-vs-run-5 delta confounds both. Experiment arm: do not merge to main.

qwen.label: Qwen 3.6 Plus
qwen.notes: DashScope's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Accepts only max_tokens. This was the default target before the registry existed; it is kept so the committed runs/qwen/ baseline stays reproducible.

qwen37.label: Qwen 3.7 Plus
qwen37.notes: Same endpoint and credential as qwen, one generation newer, so a qwen-vs-qwen37 diff is an in-family generational delta on the model this project started from. Distinct model_env (QWEN37_MODEL, not QWEN_MODEL) so pinning one snapshot cannot silently move the other.

opus5.label: Claude Opus 5
opus5.notes: Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Selected because the system card's profile — strong at vulnerability identification, weaker at exploitation — is the closest published match to this scanner's task, which is defensive static analysis rather than CTF. Shares a key and base_url_env with sonnet5 but keys its own run tree, per the key-on-the-model rule.

sonnet5.label: Claude Sonnet 5
sonnet5.notes: The mid tier most teams actually run in production, so it answers 'what will our existing stack do' rather than 'what is the ceiling'. Pairs with opus5 as an intra-vendor capability ladder, the same role terra/sol play for the GPT-5.6 family.

gemini-pro.label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
gemini-pro.notes: Google's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Third frontier lab in the comparison; without it the benchmark reads as OpenAI vs Anthropic. Confirm before a run whether a 3.5 Pro has shipped — the 3.5 line currently exposes Flash and Flash Lite only, so 3.1 Pro is the current Pro tier.

gemini-cyber.label: Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber
gemini-cyber.notes: A domain-tuned security variant rather than a general model — the only entry in the registry that is. Against gemini-pro it isolates a question nothing else here asks: whether security tuning beats raw capability on defensive static analysis. Note the published claim is on CyberGym, an offensive benchmark, so it is a hypothesis this run tests rather than evidence for the result.

kimi.label: Kimi K3
kimi.notes: Highest-scoring open-weight model on the July 2026 CyberBench snapshot (79.03%, rank 4). Publishes a 90% cached-input discount, which matters disproportionately here: a v2 run is ~3.4M input against ~0.39M output, so cache behaviour moves the bill far more than headline price does.

glm.label: GLM-5.2
glm.notes: MIT-licensed open weights, CyberBench rank 5 (77.36%). The licence is the point as much as the score: a self-hostable model is the only option for teams that cannot send proprietary source to a third-party API, which is a large share of the audience for a scanner result.

deepseek.label: DeepSeek V4
deepseek.notes: MIT-licensed, and the cost floor of the comparison by a wide margin — the V4 Flash tier is roughly two orders of magnitude below sol on input. Sets the 'how far does cheap get you' anchor. Confirm at preflight which V4 tier the model id resolves to before quoting any cost figure against it.
